topic: How a cooling system keeps a data centre running: heat source, air path, chilled water loop, heat rejection, and failure with redundancy
scope_note: How a typical enterprise or colocation data hall is cooled: heat source, air path, chilled water loop, heat rejection outdoors, failure and redundancy. Qualitative, with one sourced temperature range. Not covered: liquid cooling to the chip, immersion, energy efficiency metrics, cost.

facts.statement: Almost all of the electrical power that servers draw is turned into heat inside the room, and that heat has to be removed continuously.
facts.reference_hint: Conservation of energy; standard in ASHRAE TC 9.9 and Uptime Institute introductory material

facts.statement: The heat a data hall produces rises and falls with the electrical load of the IT equipment: more computing work means more power drawn and more heat to carry away.
facts.caveat: Say 'roughly follows'; fans, lighting and power equipment add a smaller share of heat.

facts.statement: Cooling equipment moves heat from one place to another rather than destroying it or making cold from nothing; the heat ends up outdoors.
In the hot aisle and cold aisle layout, server racks stand in rows with their fronts facing each other across a cold aisle and their backs facing each other across a hot aisle.
facts.reference_hint: ASHRAE TC 9.9 thermal guidelines; widely used layout

facts.statement: Typical air-cooled servers draw cool air in through the front and blow warmed air out of the back.
facts.caveat: Front-to-back airflow is the common convention for rack servers, not universal for every device.

facts.statement: A CRAH (computer room air handler) is a unit that blows cold air into the room and takes hot return air back in across a coil filled with chilled water.
facts.reference_hint: Vendor white papers (Schneider Electric, Vertiv); ASHRAE terminology

facts.statement: A CRAC (computer room air conditioner) does a similar air-handling job but cools the air with its own compressor and refrigerant instead of a chilled water coil.
Cold supply air is often delivered through a raised floor, rising through floor tiles in the cold aisle, though some halls supply it from overhead ducts.
Aisle containment, using doors, panels or curtains to close off the hot aisle or the cold aisle, keeps hot exhaust air from mixing with cold supply air.
facts.caveat: Containment reduces mixing; it does not remove it entirely.
facts.reference_hint: ASHRAE TC 9.9; US DOE / LBNL data centre efficiency guidance

facts.statement: When hot exhaust air mixes back into the cold supply air, some servers receive warmer air than intended, which creates hot spots and wastes cooling capacity.
facts.caveat: Effect size depends on the layout.

facts.statement: In a chilled water system, the water absorbs heat from the air at the CRAH coil and flows on warmer, while pumps keep the water circulating around the loop.
A chiller removes heat from the returning warm chilled water using a refrigeration cycle and sends the water back cold to the CRAHs.
facts.reference_hint: Vendor white papers (Schneider Electric, Vertiv); ASHRAE handbooks

facts.statement: The heat taken from the chilled water is passed to a second loop or to outdoor equipment, such as a cooling tower, a dry cooler or an air-cooled condenser, which releases it to the outdoor air.
facts.caveat: Which outdoor equipment is used depends on the site; a cooling tower rejects heat largely by evaporating some of the water, while a dry cooler uses air only.

facts.statement: Free cooling, also called an economiser, lets a site reduce or skip the chiller's compressor work when outdoor conditions are cool enough.
facts.caveat: Only available part of the year at many sites, depending on climate and design.

facts.statement: N+1 redundancy means having the number of units needed to carry the load (N) plus one extra spare, so that one unit can fail or be serviced without losing capacity.
facts.reference_hint: Uptime Institute, Tier Standard topology; vendor white papers

facts.statement: 2N redundancy means a complete duplicate of the whole system, so that one entire side can fail and the other side still carries the full load.
facts.reference_hint: Uptime Institute, Tier Standard topology; vendor white papers

facts.statement: In a redundant design, when a pump or CRAH fails, a standby unit starts or the remaining units take up the load, usually automatically through the control system.
facts.caveat: Depends on the site's design and controls; say 'in a well designed system'.

facts.statement: Temperature sensors and the monitoring system raise alarms when temperatures drift past set limits, so operators can respond before servers are affected.
facts.caveat: Alarm limits and responses are set by each site.

facts.statement: If cooling is lost and not restored, the air temperature in the hall rises, and servers may slow themselves down (throttle) or shut down to protect the hardware.
facts.caveat: How quickly this happens depends on the load and the room, so no time is stated.

facts.statement: Thermal ride-through is the time a hall stays within safe temperatures after cooling stops or changes over, helped by the chilled water held in the pipes and in buffer tanks.
facts.caveat: Duration is site-specific and limited; no figure is given.

facts.statement: ASHRAE recommends a server inlet air temperature between 18 and 27 degrees Celsius for its main data centre equipment classes.
facts.caveat: This is a recommended range for the air entering the servers, not a hard limit; a wider allowable range exists, and newer guidance for some high-density equipment differs. Say 'recommended' and 'inlet'.
facts.reference_hint: ASHRAE TC 9.9, Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments (recommended envelope, classes A1 to A4)

terms.plain: computer room air handler: a large cabinet with fans and a chilled water coil that cools the room's air
a machine that removes heat from water using a refrigeration cycle
a closed pipe circuit carrying cold water to the CRAHs and warm water back to the chiller
outdoor equipment that releases heat to the air, largely by evaporating some of the water
enough units for the load plus one spare
two complete, independent copies of the system
physical barriers that keep hot and cold air apart
the temperature of the air entering the front of a server

not_claimed: Cooling 'creates cold': it moves heat, it does not make coldness.
Any figure for what share of data centre energy goes to cooling: it varies widely by site and no figure is approved here.
Any figure for how fast a hall heats up when cooling stops: it depends on load and room, so no time is given.
That every data centre has chillers, cooling towers or a raised floor: designs differ.
That redundancy makes failure impossible: it removes single points of failure, but multiple failures or poor maintenance can still cause outages.
Named incidents or outage statistics: none are approved.
That the 18 to 27 degrees Celsius range is a hard limit that servers fail outside of.
